title: Not Original
core: All four say a work contains nothing invented — the substance came from outside the maker. What splits them is *what it came from*: one prior model, a style deliberately put on, a phrase used to death by everybody, or simply the way things are normally done. They also differ sharply in heat: two are usable as flat description, one can be outright praise, one is always a sneer.

words.nuance: **Derivative** points backward at a *source* — you could name the earlier writer, album, or painter it came out of. The charge is subtraction: the maker worked honestly but left nothing of himself in it. Coldest of the four; a diagnosis, not an attack, which is exactly why critics and examiners like it.

**Pastiche** is the only one where the imitation is *open and intended* — the borrowing is the point, not a failure. It's a noun for the object, not a verdict on it, so context decides: "a loving pastiche of Chandler" praises, "mere pastiche" damns. Also the only one that can mean a medley stitched from several sources at once.

**Hackneyed** has no single source at all — it indicts *frequency*. The thing was fresh once and got repeated until it went dead, so the fault is laziness in reaching for it. Attaches almost only to language and ideas (a phrase, a plot twist, a metaphor), never to methods or objects, and it is the one word here that is never neutral.

**Conventional** measures against the room's norms rather than against any prior work: it does what is standard, not what someone else did. Uniquely, it stays purely descriptive on procedures and equipment — conventional surgery, conventional weapons — and only turns into a quiet insult when aimed at a person's taste or an artwork.

exam_note: The trap is polarity: only *hackneyed* is reliably pejorative, so a sentence whose surrounding clues are neutral or admiring rules it out and points to *conventional*, *derivative*, or *pastiche*.
